ABSTRACT Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively mitigates the knowledge cutoff and hallucination issues of large language models by incorporating external knowledge bases. However, standard RAG applies a uniform retrieval strategy to all question types and feeds redundant retrieval results directly into the generator, leading to high token consumption and potentially degraded answer quality. This paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates questiontype-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies queries into three types—factual, definitional, and reasoning—via an LLM classifier, applies a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type, then uses a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, and finally generates answers from the compressed and refined context. To independently quantify the contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets—HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue—and evaluate using four metrics: Exact Match, F1, Recall@10, and token consumption. Experimental results show that SAC-RAG reduces token consumption by 38%–58% at the cost of only a 1–2 percentage point EM drop, with EM actually improving after compression for reasoning-type questions, achieving the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off in terms of token consumption, with a moderate increase in per-query latency due to additional LLM calls. SAC-RAG offers a modular and interpretable optimization solution for the efficient deployment of RAG in real-world settings. INDEX TERMS Context compression, multi-hop question answering, question-type-adaptive retrieval, retrieval-augmented generation, semantic classification. I. INTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, yet they suffer from two inherent limitations: knowledge cutoff and factual hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances LLM responses by retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases and has become the dominant approach for addressing these issues. However, standard RAG systems have two critical blind spots. First, they apply a uniform retrieval strategy to all questions, ignoring the fact that different question types require The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Alba Amato . differentiated retrieval approaches. On the compression side, methods such as LLMLingua [5] and LongLLMLingua compress retrieved context on top of standard retrieval, effectively reducing token consumption; however, they operate on a fixed retrieval pipeline without considering question-type differences in the retrieval stage. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work unifies question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. To address these limitations, this paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies each user query into one of three semantic types via an LLM classifier: Fact, Definition, and Reasoning. SAC-RAG employs a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type. Fact-type questions use hybrid retrieval combining BM25 sparse retrieval and Milvus dense vector retrieval with BGE cross-encoder reranking. Definition-type questions adopt pure semantic vector retrieval. Reasoning-type questions are decomposed into multiple sub-questions by an LLM, with results merged after parallel retrieval. Once retrieval is complete, results of all types pass through a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, which are then fed into the generator to produce the final answer. To systematically validate the independent contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation settings on three multi-hop question answering datasets—HotpotQA [6], 2WikiMultiHopQA [7], and MuSiQue [8]—namely Naive RAG (baseline), Compress RAG (compression only), Adaptive RAG (adaptive retrieval only), and SAC-RAG (the full framework). Evaluation covers four metrics: Exact Match (EM), F1, Recall@10, and average token consumption. Experimental results show that: (1) adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement, boosting EM from 0.560 to 0.611 ( +9.1%) and Recall@10 from 0.787 to 0.880 (+11.8%) on HotpotQA; (2) context compression reduces token consumption by 55–58% with EM decreasing by only 1–2 percentage points; (3) SAC-RAG achieves the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off; on Reasoning-type questions, EM improves after compression (HotpotQA: 0.455→0.577). Unlike previous studies that optimize either retrieval or compression independently, SAC-RAG coordinates semantic-aware retrieval and context compression within a unified framework. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • A question-semantic-type-based adaptive retrieval framework with three differentiated retrieval strategies; • A unified architecture, SAC-RAG, that integrates adaptive retrieval and context compression; • Systematic ablation experiments that independently quantify the contribution of each component, providing clear guidance for RAG system optimization. EVOLUTION OF RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced by Lewis et al. [9] in 2020, with the core idea of retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases as additional context before an LLM generates an answer, thereby addressing knowledge cutoff and hallucination. Early RAG systems relied on dense vector retrieval [10], mapping queries and documents into a shared vector space for nearest neighbor search. Gao et al. [11] categorized the evolution of RAG into three stages: Naive RAG uses a fixed retrieve-thengenerate pipeline; Advanced RAG introduces pre- and postretrieval optimizations such as query rewriting, reranking, and compression; Modular RAG decomposes the system into independently replaceable functional modules, supporting iterative retrieval and adaptive scheduling. A recent systematic review [12] further confirms this taxonomy through a PRISMA-compliant analysis of 128 highly cited RAG studies, identifying modular and policy-driven architectures as the prevailing trend. Within this framework, training paradigms such as Atlas [13], context-prefix schemes such as In-Context RALM [14], and standardized benchmarks such as BEIR [15] emerged in succession. As retrieved documents grow longer, however, LLMs become less effective at using key information in extended contexts [1]: redundant content not only raises computational cost but also introduces noise that can degrade answer quality. These issues are particularly acute in multi-hop reasoning, where retrieval spans multiple documents of uneven relevance, demanding both precision in retrieval strategies and efficiency in context utilization— as well as coordination between the two. Existing work addressing these bottlenecks falls into three main directions: adaptive retrieval, context compression, and joint optimization of retrieval and reasoning. B. ADAPTIVE RETRIEVAL METHODS Adaptive retrieval adjusts retrieval strategies based on query characteristics to obtain more precise context. For strategy selection, Adaptive-RAG [3] routes questions among no-retrieval, single-step, and multi-step retrieval paths based on question complexity; Self-RAG [16] uses a selfreflection mechanism to trigger retrieval on demand during generation; FLARE [17] actively supplements retrieval based on token confidence during decoding. For retrieval quality, V endi-RAG [18] introduces a diversity metric to balance coverage and relevance of retrieved documents; REPLUG [19] improves reliability through multi-retriever ensembling. On the input side, Ma et al. [20] proposed the Rewrite-Retrieve-Read framework, training a compact rewriting model to optimize queries before retrieval. More recently, LLM-based generation-augmented rewriting methods such as GaQR [21] further leverage chain-of-thought reasoning to expand queries, achieving substantial retrieval recall improvements. However, these routing methods primarily address model selection or query-complexity-based dispatch, whereas SAC-RAG adapts retrieval strategies within a unified pipeline according to semantic question types—a distinction that yields finergrained control over the retrieval process. A shared limitation of these methods is that their adaptation axis centers on question complexity or token confidence, without designing differentiated retrieval mechanisms based on question semantic type (factual, definitional, reasoning). As a result, retrieval strategies lack a structured understanding of the nature of the question. C. CONTEXT COMPRESSION METHODS Context compression aims to reduce redundancy in retrieval results, lowering token consumption during generation. LLMLingua [5] introduced selective compression of retrieval results using a small language model; LongLLMLingua [24] extended this to long-context settings. In terms of compression strategy, RECOMP [25] formalized compression as a summarization task; BRIEF [26] introduced a queryaware mechanism that doubles the compression rate while maintaining answer quality; LLMLingua-2 [27] proposed a task-agnostic data distillation approach. SARA [28] further combines fine-grained textual spans with compact semantic compression vectors to improve context efficiency under strict token budgets. The growing focus on token efficiency has also motivated agentic frameworks such as TeaRAG[29], which jointly compresses retrieved content and reasoning chains to achieve significant token reduction while preserving accuracy. A common limitation of these methods is that compression operates on top of a fixed retrieval strategy: the retrieval stage is unaware of downstream compression needs, and the compression stage does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage. The two components remain independent, lacking co-design. D. JOINT RETRIEVAL AND REASONING In multi-hop QA, retrieval and reasoning are not independent stages—reasoning requires multiple retrieval steps to supply intermediate evidence, and retrieval strategies shift dynamically with each reasoning step. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [30] established the approach of improving reasoning through intermediate steps; ReAct [31] interleaves reasoning and action, deciding after each reasoning step whether new retrieval is needed; IRCoT [32] embeds retrieval within each step of the CoT reasoning chain. For task decomposition, DecomP [33] and DSP [34] adopt a decompose-retrieve-merge strategy; ChainRAG [2] addresses the information loss problem in sub-question decomposition through progressive retrieval-and-rewriting over a sentence graph. KiRAG[4] further incorporates knowledge triples into iterative retrieval, bridging information gaps across reasoning steps. These works show the value of jointly optimizing retrieval and reasoning. However, they focus on retrieval–reasoning synergy, while the joint optimization of retrieval and compression remains an open problem: no existing method unifies adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. E. RESEARCH GAP AND MOTIVATION The analysis of the three directions above reveals a shared limitation: the components of a RAG system— retrieval, compression, and reasoning—are still optimized as independent modules. Adaptive retrieval addresses how to retrieve, but does not consider how the retrieval results will be compressed; context compression addresses how to condense,

E. RESEARCH GAP AND MOTIVATION The analysis of the three directions above reveals a shared limitation: the components of a RAG system— retrieval, compression, and reasoning—are still optimized as independent modules. Adaptive retrieval addresses how to retrieve, but does not consider how the retrieval results will be compressed; context compression addresses how to condense, but does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage to guide compression strategy; joint retrieval and reasoning demonstrates the value of co-design, but this principle has yet to be extended to retrieval and compression. The core motivation of SAC-RAG is to fill this gap: to build a unified framework in which question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression work together. In SAC-RAG, the classifier’s output determines the retrieval strategy; the resulting type-specific retrieval outputs naturally differ in document count, redundancy, and information density, which shapes the input to the downstream compression module. Although compression itself uses a unified prompt and logic across all question types, the diversity of its inputs produces type-adaptive compression effects. This indirect coordination through the data flow distinguishes SAC-RAG from prior modular designs where retrieval and compression operate as independently configurable modules. Retrieval strategies are differentiated by semantic type, compression processes diverse retrieval outputs with a consistent logic, and the two components achieve positive complementarity in the quality–efficiency trade-off. III. METHOD A. SAC-RAG SYSTEM OVERVIEW The SAC-RAG pipeline, as shown in Figure1, consists of five core stages: question classification, type-specific retrieval, context compression, answer generation, and evaluation. Given a user query q, the system first determines its semantic type t via a question classifier, then selects the corresponding retrieval strategy to retrieve a document set from the knowledge base D, after which a unified context compression module extracts refined evidence snippets, and the system finally generates the answer ˆa. B. QUESTION CLASSIFIER The question classifier uses an LLM with a structured prompt and few-shot examples to categorize queries into three types. C. TYPE-SPECIFIC RETRIEVAL STRATEGIES 1) FACT: HYBRID RETRIEVAL + RERANKING Fact-type questions involve specific entities and keywords. Relying solely on dense vector retrieval may miss exact term matches due to semantic generalization. SAC-RAG adopts a hybrid retrieval strategy, where the combined score for a candidate document d is defined as follows: SFact(q, d)=λ· BM25(q, d)+ (1−λ)· cos(eq, ed ) (2) where eq and ed are dense vectors of the query and document encoded by text-embedding-3-small, and the BM25 term matching score is computed as: BM25(q, d)= ∑ w∈q IDF(w)· f (w, d)(k1+ 1) f (w, d)+ k1(1− b+ b |d| avgdl ) (3) where f (w, d) is the term frequency of w in document d,|d| is the document length, avgdl is the average document length, and k1 and b are BM25 hyperparameters (default k1= 1.5, b= 0.75). The specific procedure is: 1) BM25 sparse retrieval: based on spaCy tokenization and rank_bm25.BM25Okapi, retrieving top-10 by term matching. 2) Dense vector retrieval: ANN retrieval via Milvus using Cosine similarity, retrieving top-10. 3) Merge and deduplication: the two result sets are merged and deduplicated by doc_id. 4) BGE reranking: using the bge-reranker-base crossencoder to score each candidate and selecting the top-10. 2) DEFINITION: PURE SEMANTIC RETRIEVAL Definition-type questions focus on the meaning of a single concept, where semantic vector similarity is sufficient to cover the relevant content. For definition-type questions, SAC-RAG uses only Milvus dense vector retrieval (Cosine similarity), taking the top-8 documents directly into the subsequent compression and generation stages, avoiding unnecessary hybrid retrieval overhead. 3) REASONING: SUB-QUESTION DECOMPOSITION + PARALLEL RETRIEVAL Reasoning-type questions require support from multiple knowledge points, and a single retrieval query may fail to cover all reasoning paths. E. ANSWER GENERATION The compressed context Ct is merged with the original query q and fed into the LLM to generate the final answer ˆa. All experimental groups use the same LLM configuration to ensure fair comparison. IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP A. DATASETS AND EVALUATION METRICS Experiments are conducted on three English multi-hop opendomain question answering datasets. Dataset statistics and evaluation metrics are shown in Table 1. The four evaluation metrics follow standard practices in the retrieval-augmented generation literature: EM and F1 follow the answer quality evaluation approach established by DPR [10], Recall@10 assesses retrieval quality, and average token consumption (Avg Tokens) follows the efficiency metric introduced by LLMLingua [5]. All answer quality metrics are computed after applying normalize_answer() normalization (Unicode NFKD, lowercasing, punctuation and article removal, whitespace collapsing). B. EXPERIMENTAL ENVIRONMENT The vector database uses Milvus (Collection en_doc_ chunk, 1536 dimensions, Cosine similarity), and metadata storage uses MongoDB. BM25 sparse retrieval is based on rank_bm25.BM25Okapi with spaCy tokenization. The reranker uses BGE bge-reranker-base [35]. ABLATION STUDY: DESIGN AND VERIFICATION 1) EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN To independently quantify the contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation study groups. The configuration and retrieval parameters of each group are shown in Table 4. Using Naïve RAG as the baseline, the remaining three groups incrementally build upon it: Compress RAG adds only the context compression module on top of Naïve RAG’s retrieval results, to independently quantify the contribution of compression; Adaptive RAG adds only the question classifier and type-specific retrieval strategies, to independently quantify the contribution of adaptive retrieval; SAC-RAG, as the full framework, enables both modules simultaneously, to verify their synergistic effect. This confirms that directly feeding redundant retrieval results into the generator introduces noise and wastes tokens; context compression effectively reduces both noise and cost. H2 validation: Adaptive RAG achieves significant EM improvements over Naïve RAG on all datasets (+5.1/+3.3/+4.2pp), with Recall@10 improvements of 2.5–9.3pp. This confirms that adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement—selecting a differentiated retrieval strategy based on question type significantly outperforms applying a uniform strategy to all questions. H3 validation: SAC-RAG further improves EM over Compress RAG (+2.3/+0.4/0.0pp), with Recall@10 gains of 1.9–9.3pp. Better initial retrieval provides higher-quality input for compression. On MuSiQue, SAC-RAG EM is level with Compress but Recall@10 leads substantially (+5.8pp), further confirming the value of adaptive retrieval within the compression pipeline. Taken together, SAC-RAG consistently achieves the optimal quality-efficiency tradeoff across all three datasets, trading only 1–2pp of EM for 38–58% token savings relative to Adaptive RAG. To visualize the token consumption patterns more directly, Figure 4 presents the per-query average token consumption of the four configurations across the three datasets. SAC-RAG maintains the lowest token consumption among all configurations on all datasets, while Adaptive RAG—despite achieving the best answer quality—incurs substantially higher token overhead than even the Naïve baseline. Compress RAG alone yields noticeable reductions, confirming that the compression module is the primary driver of token savings. D. ANAL YSIS OF COMPRESSION EFFECTS BY QUESTION TYPE The ablation results above validate the overall effectiveness of adaptive retrieval and context compression. However, a deeper question constitutes the theoretical premise of SAC-RAG’s design—does context compression affect different question types uniformly? If compression effects were type-independent, there would be no need for differentiated retrieval after classification; conversely, if different types respond to compression in significantly different ways, this validates the design rationale of ‘‘classify first, then retrieve’’ in SAC-RAG. To answer this question, Table 6 presents the percategory performance of Adaptive RAG and SAC-RAG across different question types. Reasoning questions represent the category where compression is most effective. On HotpotQA, SAC-RAG achieves an EM of 0.577 on Reasoning questions, a 26.8% improvement over Adaptive RAG’s 0.455. On 2Wiki, Adaptive RAG’s EM on Reasoning questions is as high as 0.859, while SAC-RAG achieves 0.855, essentially on par, with token consumption dropping from 3,255 to 1,490 (−54.2%). For questions involving multi-step reasoning chains, compression effectively filters out noise in the retrieved results, allowing the LLM to focus on critical evidence. On MuSiQue, the Reasoning EM decreases modestly from 0.253 to 0.220 (−3.3 pp), suggesting that when retrieval quality is already low (Recall@10=0.372–0.385), the compressed context may lose critical evidence fragments that are too sparse to survive filtering. Factual questions constitute the largest category by count. On both datasets, SAC-RAG’s EM on Fact questions decreases by 2.4% (HotpotQA: 0.614→0.599) and 4.9% (2Wiki: 0.528→0.502), respectively, compared to Adaptive RAG. ERROR ANAL YSIS OF COMPRESSION DEGRADATION To understand under what circumstances context compression leads to degraded answer quality, we conduct a fine-grained degradation analysis on the HotpotQA dataset. Comparing the per-question F1 scores of Adaptive RAG and SAC-RAG, the results are shown in Table 7. Definition-type questions are the most sensitive to compression. By comparing the retrieved documents before and after compression for the same question, we find that the top-8 retrieved documents are identical, ruling out retrieval differences as the cause of degradation and confirming that the issue lies in the post-compression answer generation stage. A representative case: Question: ‘‘Who is this American cartoonist, writer, producer, animator, and voice actor that worked with this multiple Shuster Award, Harvey Award and Eisner Award nominee and an Eisner Award–winning comic book creator?’’ Ground truth: Matt Groening Adaptive RAG: Matt Groening ✓ SAC-RAG: Steve Purcell ✗ The retrieval context simultaneously contains relevant documents about both Matt Groening and Steve Purcell. In the full context, the LLM correctly identifies the target person; however, in the compressed and refined context, the distinguishing cues between the two entities are weakened. This case reveals the core risk of compression for definitiontype questions: when multiple entities of the same type co-occur in the context, compression may weaken the distinguishing cues between them. Fact-type questions show a slight but systematic drop. Among 958 Fact questions, 63 (6.6%) show F1 drops. The typical degradation pattern is the loss of key factual details during compression. For instance, the question ‘‘Where was the place of death of Vigrahapala I (Pala Dynasty)’s father?’’ has the ground-truth answer Peshawar; Adaptive RAG answers correctly, while SAC-RAG incorrectly answers Bengal. Reasoning-type questions benefit from compression. Among the 22 Reasoning questions in HotpotQA, only 1 shows degradation, and SAC-RAG’s EM on the Reasoning category improves from 0.455 to 0.577 (+26.8%). CONCLUSION This paper proposes SAC-RAG, a unified framework that integrates question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG uses an LLM classifier to categorize queries in real time into factual, definitional, and reasoning types, and employs differentiated retrieval strategies for each type—Fact-type questions use hybrid BM25 and dense vector retrieval with reranking, Definition-type questions adopt pure semantic retrieval, and Reasoning-type questions undergo sub-question decomposition followed by parallel retrieval— after which all retrieval results pass through a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets before generating the final answer. Results from four progressive ablation experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue demonstrate that: (1) adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement, boosting EM by 3.3–5.1 percentage points and Recall@10 by 2.5–9.3 percentage points; (2) context compression reduces token consumption by 38–58% with EM decreasing by only 1–2 percentage points; (3) SAC-RAG achieves the optimal quality–efficiency tradeoff, lying on the Pareto frontier on all three datasets; for reasoning-type questions, compression improves answer quality by filtering out noise. The time overhead (approximately 27.8 s vs. 9.6 s per instance for Naïve RAG on HotpotQA) primarily stems from the additional LLM calls for classification, subquestion decomposition, and compression. This trade-off between token efficiency and latency should be weighed against application-specific deployability requirements. Introduction Emotion recognition is being used more and more in a applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, interactive virtual agents, and mental health monitoring because it allows the machines to understand a human affect and when compared to a conventional handcrafted feature approaches, deep learning advances greatly enhanced the performance of facial emotion recognition (FER) systems, especially on benchmark datasets like FER2013 and Extended Cohn-Kanade Dataset (CK+). Even with these improvements, many current FER solutions are primarily tested in the controlled environments and frequently fail in real-world scenarios due to the occlusion and pose, variation and changes in light. Furthermore, some systems ignore deployment factors such as resilient input processing, secure access, and real-time inference, focusing only on model accuracy. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a modular real-time facial emotion recognition system that integrates four key components such as robust face acquisition and detection, transfer-learning-based emotion classification, normalization-driven preprocessing and interpretable output visualization. The proposed framework gives a greater priority on the practical scalability, reliability, and the deployment readiness than a traditional FER system, which only considers benchmark performances. This work attempts to close the gap between theoretical emotion recognition models and their practical applications by combining multimodal inputs with robust preprocessing, lightweight deep learning models, and system-level integration. Data augmentation studies have shown that the controlled transformations can significantly reduce the overfitting and increase robustness in vision tasks like FER [12]. Label-distribution learning and crowdsourced annotation modeling were introduced to improve the training stability in noisy datasets and address ambiguity in facial emotion labels [13]. Unresolved practical issues, such as illumination sensitivity, pose variation, fairness across demographics, and poor performance in subtle emotions in real-world streams, are still reported in recent synthesis studies [14] [15]. Thus, there is a clear need in the literature for FER systems that offer stable [16] [17], comprehensible, and effective end-to-end behavior in real-world deployment environments in addition to performing well on benchmarks. A significant shift in the study of facial emotion recognition (FER) is observed from traditional machine learning methods to modern techniques using deep learning. The first studies allowed people to find faces, extract their features and group them. Datasets such as FER2013, CK+, JAFFE and AffectNet provided a benchmark for structured evaluations in controlled and real-world environments. Deep learning makes it easier for VGG, ResNet and convolutional neural networks to present and classify features. To make systems more robust and to cope with ambiguous labels, data-centric methods such as data augmentation and label distribution learning are proposed. However, there are still several challenges to overcome, including sensitivity to illumination and pose variations, class imbalance, annotation noise, and poor generalization to real-world scenarios. Existing models also have limited capacity in detecting subtle emotion and are not fair among diverse demographic groups. These limitations point to the need for more robust, scalable and interpretable FER systems which can operate reliably in unconstrained settings, motivating the approach proposed in this work. Keyser,* and Denis Garoli* Cite This:ACSNano 2022, 16, 17552−17571 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: With the total amount of worldwide data skyrocketing, the global data storage demand is predicted to grow to 1.75 × 1014 GB by 2025. Traditional storage methods have difficulties keeping pace given that current storage media have a maximum density of 103 GB/mm3. As such, data production will far exceed the capacity of currently available storage methods. The costs of maintaining and transferring data, as well as the limited lifespans and significant data losses associated with current technologies also demand advanced solutions for information storage. Nature offers a powerful alternative through the storage of information that defines living organisms in unique orders of four bases (A, T, C, G) located in molecules called deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). DNA molecules as information carriers have many advantages over traditional storage media. Their high storage density, potentially low maintenance cost, ease of synthesis, and chemical modification make them an ideal alternative for information storage. To this end, rapid progress has been made over the past decade by exploiting user-defined DNA materials to encode information. In this review, we discuss the most recent advances of DNA-based data storage with a major focus on the challenges that remain in this promising field, including the current intrinsic low speed in data writing and reading and the high cost per byte stored. Alternatively, data storage relying on DNA nanostructures (as opposed to DNA sequence) as well as on other combinations of nanomaterials and biomolecules are proposed with promising technological and economic advantages. In summarizing the advances that have been made and underlining the challenges that remain, we provide a roadmap for the ongoing research in this rapidly growing field, which will enable the development of technological solutions to the global demand for superior storage methodologies. Assessing Digital Data Storage in Microbial Genomes Through Statistical Simulation Abstract—DNA can carry digital information in a compact form. When that information is placed inside a living microbe, it can also be copied as the organism reproduces. The difficulty is keeping the stored sequence unchanged. Mutations, random changes in a population, and differences in growth can gradually make the data unreadable. This paper describes a simulation that examines these effects together. A 4 kB file is divided into indexed DNA fragments with error-detection fields, stored with different levels of redundancy, and followed through a model of microbial evolution. Recovery is estimated by sampling reads and applying a simplified consensus decoder. The reported experiments use 200 repetitions and mutation rates between 10-7 and 10-5 per base per generation. Extra copies improve recovery when the payload is neutral, but their benefit is much smaller when damaged variants have a growth advantage. Increasing sequencing depth helps at low coverage, although it cannot restore a sequence that has already disappeared. The results describe the behaviour of the model; they do not establish storage lifetimes for an engineered organism. Index Terms— DNA storage; microbial genomes; simulation; mutation; genetic drift; redundancy; data recovery. I. INTRODUCTION An archive is useful only if its contents remain readable. Conventional storage systems need maintenance, replacement hardware, and occasional transfers to newer formats. DNA offers another way to represent information: digital symbols can be mapped to nucleotide sequences and later reconstructed from sequencing reads. Its potential density makes it attractive for data that are kept for long periods and accessed infrequently. Most DNA storage approaches treat the molecules as material kept outside living cells. Genomic storage adds a different possibility. Once an encoded sequence is introduced into a microbial genome, cell division can produce further copies. This makes replication part of the storage process, but it also brings biological change into the system. A descendant may carry a damaged version of the original message, and a variant that grows faster may become common even when it no longer preserves the data. The practical question is therefore how much of a file can be recovered after a given number of generations. This study examines the roles of mutation, redundancy, selection, and sequencing coverage. It uses a population model to explore their combined effects before attempting biological validation. II. BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION Cell-free storage methods use techniques such as overlapping fragments, error-correcting codes, constrained sequence design, and protective packaging. Storage in living organisms must address another problem: the carrier changes while it makes copies. Earlier demonstrations show that structured information can be placed in cellular DNA, but demonstrating storage is different from establishing reliable recovery over many generations. A simulation makes it possible to vary individual assumptions and compare outcomes under controlled conditions. Here, a neutral population model provides a useful baseline, while selection tests how strongly a small growth advantage for damaged variants can change the result. III. STORAGE MODEL AND ENCODING The workflow has four stages: convert the file into DNA fragments, assign copies to storage locations, propagate the population, and attempt recovery at fixed checkpoints. It separates inherited damage from errors introduced during sequencing. This distinction matters because deeper sequencing may reduce sampling uncertainty, whereas it cannot recreate an original sequence that has been lost from the population. A. Fragment structure The file is divided into blocks of 160 bits. Each block occupies an 80-nucleotide payload field under a two-bits-per-base mapping. A 12-nucleotide index records the block position, and an 8-nucleotide cyclic redundancy check (CRC) provides error detection. Each complete fragment therefore contains 100 nucleotides. With 200 fragments, the payload is 32,000 bits, or 4,000 bytes. It does not enforce limits on repeated bases or other sequence constraints that may be needed in practice. The resulting density should therefore be read as an idealised value. Real genomic copies can have linked histories and can be affected together by large deletions or recombination, so independence is an approximation. C. Mutation probability Let u denote the per-base probability of a damaging change in one generation, and let L be the fragment length. The chance that at least one base in a fragment changes is: q = 1 - (1 - u)L ≈ Lu (1) The approximation is useful when Lu is small. In this model, any damaging change moves a fragment from an intact state into a mutated state. Reverse changes that restore the exact original fragment are omitted. Insertions and deletions are not represented explicitly; their possible effects are absorbed into the overall damage probability. Consequently, the model tracks whether a fragment is intact rather than the detailed sequence of every mutant. D. Selection and genetic drift For each fragment copy, x of the P cells carry a mutated variant, giving a mutant frequency p = x/P. Intact variants have relative fitness 1 and mutated variants have fitness 1 + s. A positive s therefore represents an advantage assigned to the mutated state. The selection step is followed by mutation: psel = p(1 + s) / [p(1 + s) + 1 - p] (2) pnext = psel + (1 - psel)q (3) The next generation is drawn as xnext ~ Binomial(P, pnext). This sampling step represents genetic drift: even with the same expected frequency, chance produces different outcomes across repetitions. The setting s = 0.01 gives every damaged state a 1% fitness advantage in the model. It does not mean that every real mutation would remove an equivalent biological burden. IV. A read is drawn from the mutated part of the population with probability p. With a per-base sequencing error probability e, the chance of reading a complete L-base fragment without a sequencing error is (1 - e)L. The simplified decoder compares correctly read intact fragments with correctly read mutant fragments. It accepts the intact sequence only when the intact count is strictly larger. A tie or failure is treated as an erasure. Random sequencing errors are assumed not to form a competing consensus, while reads assigned to a mutant lineage are assumed to agree. The useful choice depends on the required recovery level and storage duration. In the reported neutral cases, moving from one copy to two provides a substantial improvement. Under selection, even four copies may be inadequate. A design should therefore consider the biological effect of the inserted sequence alongside its coding scheme. Maximising the number of copies alone is not enough. VIII. LIMITATIONS AND INTERPRETATION The model deliberately reduces a complex biological system to a small set of states. This makes the experiment manageable, but it also limits the conclusions. The results are most useful for comparing assumptions within the model and identifying questions for later experiments. A. Damage and decoding are simplified All damaging changes are grouped into one mutated state. Actual substitutions, insertions, deletions, and rearrangements can affect a payload differently. Some may be corrected by a suitable code, while others can destroy the index or several adjacent fragments. Treating every changed fragment as unusable can be pessimistic in some situations. On the other hand, assuming perfect error detection and uncomplicated consensus can be optimistic. The overall bias cannot be described by a single direction.

B. Genomic copies may fail together Separate copies are treated as independent mutation processes, although copies inside the same genome share inheritance and can be affected by linked events. Recombination between repeated sequences, large deletions, or a population bottleneck could remove several copies together. Such events would reduce the protection expected from independent repetition. C. Population size and fitness need further study The population contains 1,000 cells throughout each run. Larger populations can have different transient behaviour even when a neutral long-run substitution-rate benchmark is unchanged. The model also gives the same fitness advantage to all mutated states. In a real organism, many mutations would not relieve the cost of carrying a payload, and some could make growth worse. A more detailed fitness model would be needed before interpreting the selection setting as a measured biological burden. D. Density and lifetime estimates are conditional The two-bit mapping leaves out sequence constraints and any additional coding overhead required for synthesis and recovery. The reported density values therefore do not describe a complete physical storage system. Likewise, the elevated mutation-rate experiments do not directly establish long-term behaviour at ordinary rates. Horizontal gene transfer, handling losses, fluctuating growth conditions, and laboratory bottlenecks are outside the model. E. Reproducibility and biological validation Independent reproduction would require the simulator, exact random seeds, decoder implementation, and configuration files. Raw outputs would also allow confidence intervals and variability to be assessed. The present results have not been validated against sequencing measurements from an engineered strain. Such validation is necessary before making practical reliability claims. IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK The simulation shows how microbial data storage can be studied as a recovery problem shaped by mutation, drift, selection, and sampling. Within the tested settings, repeated copies improve the survival of neutral payloads. A growth advantage for damaged variants sharply reduces that benefit. Sequencing depth helps when reads are scarce, but its value becomes limited once inherited damage is widespread. A useful next version would represent explicit sequence changes, linked copies, realistic fitness effects, and population bottlenecks. It could also compare repetition with an outer error-correcting code and incorporate sequence-design constraints. Most importantly, its predictions should be compared with observed recovery from biological samples. Until then, the framework provides a way to examine design trade-offs rather than a demonstrated guarantee of durable genomic storage.

Lowe, Member, IEEE Abstract—For many computer vision and machine learning problems, large training sets are key for good performance. However, the most computationally expensive part of many computer vision and machine learning algorithms consists of finding nearest neighbor matches to high dimensional vectors that represent the training data. We propose new algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor matching and evaluate and compare them with previous algorithms. For matching high dimensional features, we find two algorithms to be the most efficient: the randomized k-d forest and a new algorithm proposed in this paper, the priority search k-means tree. We also propose a new algorithm for matching binary features by searching multiple hierarchical clustering trees and show it outperforms methods typically used in the literature. We show that the optimal nearest neighbor algorithm and its parameters depend on the data set characteristics and describe an automated configuration procedure for finding the best algorithm to search a particular data set. In order to scale to very large data sets that would otherwise not fit in the memory of a single machine, we propose a distributed nearest neighbor matching framework that can be used with any of the algorithms described in the paper. All this research has been released as an open source library called fast library for approximate nearest neighbors (FLANN), which has been incorporated into OpenCV and is now one of the most popular libraries for nearest neighbor matching. In practice the time-constrained approximation criterion has been found to give better results than the error-constrained approximate search. Multiple randomized k-d trees are proposed in [13] as a means to speed up approximate nearest-neighbor search. In [14] we perform a wide range of comparisons showing that the multiple randomized trees are one of the most effective methods for matching high dimensional data. Variations of the k-d tree using non-axis-aligned_ partitioning hyperplanes have been proposed: the PCA-tree [15], the RP-tree [16], and the trinary projection tree [17]. We have not found such algorithms to be more efficient than a randomized k-d tree decomposition, as the overhead of evaluating multiple dimensions during search outweighed the benefit of the better space decomposition. Another class of partitioning trees decompose the space using various clustering algorithms instead of using hyperplanes as in the case of the k-d tree and its variants. Example of such decompositions include the hierarchical k-means tree [18], the GNAT [19], the anchors hierarchy [20], the vptree [21], the cover tree [22] and the spill-tree [23]. [25] propose a ball-tree data structure constructed using a mixed partitional-agglomerative clustering algorithm. Schindler et al. [26] propose a new way of searching the hierarchical k-means tree. Philbin et al. [2] conducted experiments showing that an approximate flat vocabulary outperforms a vocabulary tree in a recognition task. Variants of LSH such as multi-probe LSH [30] improves the high storage costs by reducing the number of hash tables, and LSH Forest [31] adapts better to the data without requiring hand tuning of parameters. The performance of hashing methods is highly dependent on the quality of the hashing functions they use and a large body of research has been targeted at improving hashing methods by using data-dependent hashing functions computed using various learning techniques: parameter sensitive hashing [5], spectral hashing [32], randomized LSH hashing from learned metrics [33], kernelized LSH [34], learnt binary embeddings [35], shift-invariant kernel hashing [36], semi-supervised hashing [37], optimized kernel hashing [38] and complementary hashing [39]. The different LSH algorithms provide theoretical guarantees on the search quality and have been successfully used in a number of projects, however our experiments reported in Section 4, show that in practice they are usually outperformed by algorithms using space partitioning structures such as the randomized k-d trees and the priority search k-means tree. 2.1.3 Nearest Neighbor Graph Techniques Nearest neighbor graph methods build a graph structure in which points are vertices and edges connect each point to its nearest neighbors. The query points are used to explore this graph using various strategies in order to get closer to their nearest neighbors. In [40] the authors select a few well separated elements in the graph as “seeds” and start the graph exploration from those seeds in a best-first fashion. Similarly, the authors of [41] perform a bestfirst exploration of the k-NN graph, but use a hill-climbing strategy and pick the starting points at random. They present recent experiments that compare favourably to randomized KD-trees, so the proposed algorithm should be considered for future evaluation and possible incorporation into FLANN. The nearest neighbor graph methods suffer from a quite expensive construction of the k-NN graph structure. Wang et al. [42] improve the construction cost by building an approximate nearest neighbor graph. 2.2 Automatic Configuration of NN Algorithms There have been hundreds of papers published on nearest neighbor search algorithms, but there has been little systematic comparison to guide the choice among algorithms and set their internal parameters. There has been extensive research on algorithm configuration methods [44], [45], however we are not aware of papers that apply such techniques to finding optimum parameters for nearest neighbor algorithms. Bergstra and Bengio [46] show that, except for small parameter spaces, random search can be a more efficient strategy for parameter optimization than grid search. 3 Fast APPROXIMATE NN MATCHING Exact search is too costly for many applications, so this has generated interest in approximate nearest-neighbor search algorithms which return non-optimal neighbors in some cases, but can be orders of magnitude faster than exact search. After evaluating many different algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor search on data sets with a wide range of dimensionality [14], [47], we have found that one of two algorithms gave the best performance: the priority search k-means tree or the multiple randomized k-d trees. These algorithms are described in the remainder of this section. 3.1. The Randomized k-d Tree Algorithm The randomized k-d tree algorithm [13], is an approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm that builds multiple randomized k-d trees which are searched in parallel. The trees are built in a similar manner to the classic k-d tree [9], [10], with the difference that where the classic kd-tree algorithm splits data on the dimension with the highest variance, for the randomized k-d trees the split dimension is chosen randomly from the top Np dimensions with the highest variance. We used the fixed value Np = 5 in our implementation, as this performs well across all our data sets and does not benefit significantly from further tuning. When searching the randomized k-d forest, a single priority queue is maintained across all the randomized trees. The priority queue is ordered by increasing distance to the decision boundary of each branch in the queue, so the search will explore first the closest leaves from all the trees. Once a data point has been examined (compared to the query point) inside a tree, it is marked in order to not be reexamined in another tree. The degree of approximation is determined by the maximum number of leaves to be visited (across all trees), returning the best nearest neighbor candidates found up to that point. The priority search k-means tree tries to better exploit the natural structure existing in the data, by clustering the data points using the full distance across all dimensions, in contrast to the (randomized) k-d tree algorithm which only partitions the data based on one dimension at a time. Nearest-neighbor algorithms that use hierarchical partitioning schemes based on clustering the data points have been previously proposed in the literature [18], [19], [24]. These algorithms differ in the way they construct the partitioning tree (whether using k-means, agglomerative or some other form of clustering) and especially in the strategies used for exploring the hierarchical tree. We have developed an improved version that explores the k-means tree using a best-bin-first strategy, by analogy to what has been found to significantly improve the performance of the approximate kd-tree searches. 3.2.1 Algorithm Description The priority search k-means tree is constructed by partitioning the data points at each level into K distinct regions using k-means clustering, and then applying the same method recursively to the points in each region. The recursion is stopped when the number of points in a region is smaller than K (see Algorithm 1). Construction time complexity. During the construction of the k-means tree, a k-means clustering operation has to be performed for each inner node. Considering a node v with n, associated data points, and assuming a maximum number of iterations J in the k-means clustering loop, the complexity of the clustering operation is O(n,dK1), where d represents the data dimensionality. Taking into account all the inner nodes ona level, we have }> n, = n, so the complexity of constructing a level in the tree is O(ndK1). Assuming a balanced tree, the height of the tree will be (log n/log K), resulting in a total tree construction cost of O(ndKI(log n/log K)). Search time complexity. In case of the time constrained approximate nearest neighbor search, the algorithm stops after examining L data points. Considering a complete priority search kmeans tree with branching factor K, the number of top down tree traversals required is L/K (each leaf node contains K points in a complete k-means tree). During each top-down traversal, the algorithm needs to check O(log n/log K) inner nodes and one leaf node. For each internal node, the algorithm has to find the branch closest to the query point, so it needs to compute the distances to all the cluster centres of the child nodes, an O(Kd) operation. The unexplored branches are added to a priority queue, which can be accomplished in O(K) amortized cost when using binomial heaps. For the leaf node the distance between the query and all the points in the leaf needs to be computed which takes O( Kd) time. In summary the overall search cost is O(Ld(log n/log K)). 3.3 The Hierarchical Clustering Tree Matching binary features is of increasing interest in the computer vision community with many binary visual descriptors being recently proposed: BRIEF [49], ORB [50], BRISK [51]. Many algorithms suitable for matching vector based features, such as the randomized kd-tree and priority search kmeans tree, are either not efficient or not suitable for matching binary features (for example, the priority search k-means tree requires the points to be in a vector space where their dimensions can be independently averaged). Binary descriptors are typically compared using the Hamming distance, which for binary data can be computed as a bitwise XOR operation followed by a bit count on the result (very efficient on computers with hardware support for counting the number of bits set in a word"). In FLANN we used the approach of performing distributed nearest neighbor search across multiple machines. 5.1 Searching on a Compute Cluster In order to scale to very large data sets, we use the approach of distributing the data to multiple machines in a compute cluster and perform the nearest neighbor search using all the machines in parallel. The data is distributed equally between the machines, such that for a cluster of N machines each of them will only have to index and search 1/N of the whole data set (although the ratios can be changed to have more data on some machines than others). The final result of the nearest neighbor search is obtained by merging the partial results from all the machines in the cluster once they have completed the search. In order to distribute the nearest neighbor matching on a compute cluster we implemented a Map-Reduce like algorithm using the message passing interface (MPI) specification. Algorithm 4 describes the procedure for building a distributed nearest neighbor matching index. Each process in the cluster executes in parallel and reads from a distributed filesystem a fraction of the data set. All processes build the nearest neighbor search index in parallel using their respective data set fractions. In order to search the distributed index the query is sent from a client to one of the computers in the MPI cluster, which we call the master server (see Fig. 13). By convention the master server is the process with rank 0 in the MPI cluster, however any process in the MPI cluster can play the role of master server. The master server broadcasts the query to all of the processes in the cluster and then each process can run the nearest neighbor matching in parallel on its own fraction of the data. When the search is complete an MPI reduce operation is used to merge the results back to the master process and the final result is returned to the client. The master server is not a bottleneck when merging the results. The MPI reduce operation is also distributed, as the partial results are merged two by two in a hierarchical fashion from the servers in the cluster to the master server. Additionally, the merge operation is very efficient, since the distances between the query and the neighbors don’t have to be re-computed as they are returned by the nearest neighbor search operations on each server. We present and compare the algorithms we have found to work best at fast approximate search in high dimensional spaces: the randomized k-d trees and a newly introduced algorithm, the priority search k-means tree. Test Research Paper: IoT-Based Smart Irrigation Purpose This synthetic test paper describes an IoT smart irrigation prototype. It is designed for testing document upload, retrieval, citations, and multi-document comparison. System Design The prototype uses a soil-moisture sensor, an ESP32 microcontroller, a relay module, and a water pump. The sensor is sampled every 30 seconds. When soil moisture falls below 35 percent, the controller switches the pump on. The pump switches off when moisture reaches 55 percent. This hysteresis band helps reduce rapid switching. Connectivity and Data The ESP32 sends timestamped moisture readings and pump states to a local dashboard over Wi-Fi using HTTP. If Wi-Fi is unavailable, local threshold-based operation continues and up to 500 readings are stored in a circular buffer. Evaluation Plan A proposed seven-day test compares water use against a fixed-timer irrigation baseline. Metrics include total water consumed, time below the 35 percent moisture threshold, pump activation count, and missing sensor readings. No measured experimental results are claimed. Limitations The prototype has not been field-validated. Sensor calibration may vary with soil type, salinity, and placement. The HTTP dashboard is intended for a trusted local network and does not define production-grade authentication. Quick Facts Controller: ESP32. Sampling interval: 30 seconds. Pump ON threshold: below 35 percent. Pump OFF threshold: 55 percent. Offline buffer: 500 readings. Proposed evaluation duration: seven days.

UNKNOWN: An Evidence-Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery Abstract—Researchers must find relevant papers, judge whether the available evidence is sufficient, detect disagreement among sources, and check their own documents against the current literature. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems usually return one fused answer and leave these judgments to the reader. This paper presents UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system in which an evidence-sufficiency signal controls retrieval and answer generation. A query is decomposed into sub-questions; each is scored for sufficiency, and insufficient ones are reformulated, searched in additional sources, or reported as gaps. Every atomic claim in a generated answer, including numbers, dates and named entities, is checked against its cited passage and repaired or removed. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status, conflicting evidence is reported with both sides, and statements in a user’s document are compared with the literature. Ablations show [which components contribute most]. Index Terms—Evidence sufficiency, retrieval-augmented generation, claim verification, conflict-aware retrieval, scholarly question answering, research-gap analysis. I. INTRODUCTION Research relies on reading many papers. The answer to a literature question is rarely contained in one snippet: a definition may come from one paper, a number from another and a limitation from a third, and the papers may disagree. A system must therefore decide whether it has enough evidence and whether that evidence can be trusted before it answers. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces unsupported answers by conditioning a language model on retrieved passages [1]. Four problems remain. First, an answer is generated even when the retrieved evidence is weak or irrelevant [2]. Second, a generated sentence may contain a number, date or name that is absent from the cited passage. Third, when papers disagree, the answer tends to blend the conflicting statements. Fourth, a user’s own document is not systematically checked against the literature. Lexical ranking with BM25 and dense retrieval over a FAISS index are standard and complementary [3]–[8]. UNKNOWN uses them as a base and does not claim them as a contribution. The contribution is the control layer around retrieval and generation: 1. Sufficiency-controlled retrieval. Evidence sufficiency is computed per sub-question across independent sources and decides whether to answer, search again, or report a gap. 2. Claim-level verification with repair. Atomic claims, including numbers, dates and names, are checked against the cited passage and corrected or removed. 3. Conflict-aware, reliability-weighted evidence. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status; disagreements are reported with both sides and a likely cause. 4. Document-versus-literature comparison. Statements in a user’s document are compared with external literature to expose outdated or contradicted claims. A typed research-gap report and evidence-linked visual tools (concept map, Knowledge DNA, 3D orbit view) are supporting features described in Section IV but not evaluated as core contributions. We do not claim to be the first scholarly question-answering system. The claim is

II. RELATED WORK A. Retrieval and Adaptive Retrieval BM25 ranks passages by term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalization [6]. Dense retrievers compare embeddings and match paraphrases [4], [5], and FAISS supports efficient nearest-neighbor search [7]. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without requiring comparable scores [8], and the behavior of fusion functions has been analyzed in detail [9]. Hybrid RAG with re-ranking has also been studied in an IEEE conference paper [10], and a survey covers RAG extensions [11]. Self-RAG, CRAG and Adaptive-RAG adapt when and how to retrieve by critiquing retrieved passages or by selecting a strategy from question complexity [12]–[14]. Work on sufficient context reports that language models frequently answer even when the provided context is insufficient [2]. These works show that multi-round and adaptive retrieval is established. They do not compute sufficiency per sub-question over independent scholarly sources, nor connect that measurement to a gap report. B. Scholarly Question Answering PaperQA2 and OpenScholar answer scientific questions with citations to papers [15], [16]; Elicit and Consensus are commercial tools for literature search and synthesis [17], [18]. Knowledge-graph methods can structure extracted knowledge for LLMs [19]. In the sources we reviewed, these systems do not compare a user’s own document with the literature or repair individual claims. C. Claim Verification and Conflicting Evidence Attribution studies ask whether generated text is supported by its sources [20]. FEVER and SciFact formalize claim verification against evidence [21], [22], and ALCE and FActScore evaluate citation quality and atomic factual precision [23], [24]. VeriCite applies natural language inference to improve citations in RAG [25], and a fake-news framework retrieves external evidence to verify extracted claims [26]. Surveys explain why generated text drifts from sources [27]. Numeric and date verification inside scholarly answers has received less attention. D. For a query q, the system must return an answer a, a verdict for each sub-question, and a report of conflicts, document-versus-literature differences and gaps, such that every assertion in the output is supported by a passage in D or is removed. The query is decomposed into sub-questions q1, ..., qm. For each, the retriever returns evidence Ei, and the sufficiency test assigns one of three statuses: sufficient, weak or insufficient. B. Research Questions RQ1. Compared with single-pass hybrid retrieval using the same retriever, does sufficiency-controlled retrieval improve answer accuracy and reduce unsupported claims? RQ2. How accurately does claim-level verification identify unsupported claims, and what share is repaired or removed? RQ3. Do reliability-weighted conflict reporting and document-versus-literature comparison surface known disagreements and seeded outdated statements? RQ4. What latency and cost does the full pipeline add relative to the base retriever and to a general-purpose assistant given the same documents? IV. METHODOLOGY A. System Overview Fig. 1 shows the pipeline. Documents are ingested, chunked and indexed. A query is analyzed and decomposed, and evidence is retrieved from the user’s library and from open scholarly sources. Each sub-question is checked for sufficiency, selected evidence is weighted for reliability and compared across sources, an answer is generated from the selected passages only, and every claim is verified. The comparison, gap report and visual tools are generated from the verified evidence. Fig. 1. UNKNOWN pipeline. Shaded stages are the contributions of this work. B. Ingestion and Chunking TXT, DOCX and PDF files are converted to text, and OCR is applied to pages without a text layer. The text is split into overlapping chunks that store the document name, title, page number, chunk number and a content hash. This metadata is kept through all later stages so that every output can be traced to its source. C. Hybrid Retrieval Base For each sub-question, BM25 [6] ranks the chunk index and a dense retriever ranks the FAISS [7] index built with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 [4], [32]. The two ranked lists are fused by reciprocal rank fusion [8]: score(c) = Σ*L* 1 / (k + rank*L*(c)) (1) where L ranges over the two lists and k is a smoothing constant. This base is identical in all experiments. D. Sufficiency-Controlled Retrieval For sub-question qi, let Ei be the top fused chunks and ni the number of independent source papers among them (chunks from one paper count once, and papers that reuse each other’s results are merged). Let ri be the mean relevance of Ei to qi, scored by [cross-encoder model] [33] and normalized to [0, 1]. The status is status(qi) = sufficient if ni ≥ τn and ri ≥ τr (2) weak if ni ≥ 1 and ri ≥ τr/2; insufficient otherwise The thresholds τn and τr are tuned on a development split and reported in Section VII. Algorithm 1 gives the control loop and Fig. 2 its decision logic. An insufficient sub-question is reformulated and searched in additional sources for at most T rounds. If it remains insufficient, it is reported as a gap and the generator is not allowed to answer it from its own memory. Fig. 2. Decision logic of the sufficiency check for one sub-question. E. A claim is supported only if three checks pass: the passage entails the claim according to [NLI model]; every number and date in the claim appears in the passage after normalization of units and formats; and every named entity in the claim appears in the passage. A failed claim is regenerated from the passage alone and checked again; if it fails twice it is removed. Algorithm 2 summarizes the procedure. F. Reliability Weighting and Conflict Reporting Each source s receives a weight w(s) = 0 if s is retracted w(s) = αV(s) + βR(s) + γC(s) otherwise (3) with α + β + γ = 1 and α, β > γ so that citation count has the smallest influence. V(s) is a venue score [source of venue scores], R(s) = exp(−λΔt) decays with the age Δt of the paper in years, and C(s) = log(1 + cites)/log(1 + citesmax). Retraction status is read from metadata when available. When two evidence sets contradict each other on the same sub-question, as judged by [NLI model], both are shown with their weights and a candidate cause extracted from metadata, such as year, dataset or method. G. Document-Versus-Literature Comparison Statements from the user’s document are aligned with statements on the same topic retrieved from Do. Each aligned pair is labeled agree, disagree or not addressed. For a disagree pair, both statements are shown with their reliability weights, which can reveal outdated or contradicted claims. H. Typed Research-Gap Report Candidate gaps are stored in three lists: limitations stated by the authors, gaps inferred across several papers, and future directions. An inferred gap is listed only with its supporting evidence and rationale, because an author-stated limitation is not necessarily a research gap. Each entry carries its document, page, chunk and sufficiency status. I. Evidence-Linked Interface The overview, Knowledge DNA, mind map and 3D orbit view are generated from concepts and relations extracted from retrieved chunks. A node or edge is kept only if a retrieved chunk supports it, and it stores the document, page and chunk. This does not remove extraction errors; it makes them traceable. V. Entailment and number matching can fail on paraphrase and implicit claims, and the cited passage itself may be wrong. Reliability weights. Venue and recency are imperfect proxies for quality, and retraction metadata may be incomplete; weights need tuning and bias checks. Comparison and gaps. Aligning a statement with the literature can misjudge scope, and an inferred gap needs expert confirmation. Model confidence is not a calibrated probability. Extraction. A supported node is not necessarily a correct extraction. Data and models. Only open-access text and abstracts are used, so coverage is partial; language-model output is not fully deterministic; any model-based judge can be biased; and the evaluated domains may not represent all fields. Scope. The typed gap report and the visual tools were not evaluated quantitatively. IX. UNKNOWN: An Evidence Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery I. Abstract Researchers must locate relevant papers, judge whether the retrieved evidence is enough, notice when sources disagree, and check their own documents against the literature; retrieval-augmented systems usually return one fused answer and leave these judgments to the reader. This paper presents UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system in which an evidence-sufficiency signal controls retrieval and answer generation. Each sub-question is scored for sufficiency, and a failure triggers query reformulation, source expansion or an explicit gap report. Every atomic claim, including its numbers, dates and names, is checked against its cited passage and repaired or removed. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status, disagreements are reported together with their likely cause, and the user's own document is compared with the open literature. Research gaps are reported in three typed categories, and the overview, Knowledge DNA, mind map and 3D concept orbit show only content backed by a linked source passage. Retrieval combines BM25 and FAISS with reciprocal rank fusion inside per-user isolated workspaces, and a single deterministic confidence score is computed in the backend. The prototype is built with Python, FastAPI and Streamlit and passes 304 backend tests. The effect of the new stages has not yet been measured; the paper specifies the baselines, public benchmarks, ablations and user study that will test it. Keywords— Evidence sufficiency, retrieval-augmented generation, claim verification, conflict-aware retrieval, document-versus-literature comparison, research-gap analysis, scholarly question answering, confidence calibration. II. Introduction Research is based on reading multiple articles. Answers to a literature query are rarely confined to one snippet since an answer might require definitions from different documents, numbers from other papers, and limitations from yet another article, and all those papers might contradict each other. Thus, document retrieval alone is not sufficient since the reader has to determine whether there is enough evidence to provide an answer and whether it is credible. Scholarly search engines index papers at very large scale and rank them with text-match, citation and recency signals, but their output is a list of papers that the reader must still open, read and reconcile. Free catalogues such as OpenAlex [1] and the Semantic Scholar platform [2] now expose metadata, abstracts and citation links through public interfaces, so an answering layer can be built on open data. What such a layer still lacks is not access to papers but a disciplined way to decide when the retrieved evidence is enough, which statements it really supports, and where it disagrees with the reader's own document. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) eliminates unfounded answers by providing a language model with retrieved passages [3]. Yet, existing RAG systems fail to solve the following four problems. First, an answer is generated out of the retrieved document regardless of how little or irrelevant this document is. Second, a generated sentence might mention a number, date or person which is not included in the retrieved passage. Third, when papers contradict each other, an answer tends to

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) eliminates unfounded answers by providing a language model with retrieved passages [3]. Yet, existing RAG systems fail to solve the following four problems. First, an answer is generated out of the retrieved document regardless of how little or irrelevant this document is. Second, a generated sentence might mention a number, date or person which is not included in the retrieved passage. Third, when papers contradict each other, an answer tends to be an amalgamation of two contradicting facts. Fourth, if a user uploads his/her own document, the system fails to check it systematically against other literature. BM25-based lexical ranking and sentence embedding-based dense retrieval with the FAISS index are baseline methods, and both have examples that the other method can miss [4]–[6]. We employ them as the retrieval component without claiming them as a novel contribution. Our novel contribution is the control mechanism around the retrieval and generation processes. Contributions include: 1. Retrieval controlled by evidence sufficiency. Sufficiency is calculated for each sub-question across independent sources and leads to deciding to answer, re-search or report a gap, so abstention becomes a retrieval indicator, not a late decision. 2. Claim-level verification with repair. Atomic claims, consisting of numbers, dates and names, are compared against the cited passage and corrected or deleted. 3. Conflict-aware, reliability-weighed evidence. Sources are weighed based on their venue, recency and retraction status; citation count is only a weak signal. Disagreements are provided with both parties and reasons for it. 4. Document vs world comparison. The answer compares the user’s document with the web and literature, stating the agreements and discrepancies, which helps identify outdated and false claims. 5. Three-type report of research gap. The author-stated limits, gaps and directions are kept separate and are linked to document, page and chunk, as well as sufficiency. 6. Evidence-related understanding tools. The overview, Knowledge DNA, mind map and 3D orbit view have only concepts and relations supported by retrieved evidence, and adjusted to students and researchers, excluding unsupported nodes. 7. Isolated, deletable knowledge workspaces. Each user and workspace owns separate lexical and vector indexes, files, metadata and history, so a query can reach only the documents in its declared scope, and deleting a document removes its chunks, vectors and derived artifacts. 8. One deterministic confidence score. A single backend formula combines sufficiency, entailment rate, source reliability and source agreement, and the score is returned with its breakdown for every feature. The claim lies in their particular combination and its demonstrated usefulness; the metric is described in Section VII and has not yet been carried out. III. Literature Review A. Retrieval and adaptive retrieval BM25 retrieves passages based on term frequency, inverse document frequency and normalization [7]. Dense retrievers compare passage embeddings and match paraphrases [5], [6]; FAISS enables efficient nearest-neighbours searching [8]. Rank fusion combines the ranked lists without needing compatible scores [9]. Retrieval-augmented generation was originally proposed for knowledge-rich language understanding tasks [3], and a survey discusses its extensions [10]. A cross-encoder re-ranker, which reads the query and the passage jointly, can refine the top candidates [11]; UNKNOWN treats it as an optional stage that is tested in the ablations. Self-RAG, CRAG, and Adaptive-RAG adapt when and how to retrieve by critiquing retrieved passages or selecting retrieval strategies by question difficulty [12]–[14]. STEEL, a fake news detection system, re-retrieves when first retrieved evidence is insufficient [15]. These works demonstrate that multiple rounds of retrieval have been done before. The works did not evaluate evidence sufficiency per sub-question from independent scholarly sources, nor did they relate the sufficiency measurement to a gap report. B. Scholarly question answering PaperQA2 and OpenScholar provide scientific answers using references to papers [16], [17]. Elicit and Consensus are tools for searching and synthesizing literature. These systems do not base answers on a user’s personal document and a set format, and, in the references provided, they do not mend claims and compare a document to literature. Open infrastructure such as OpenAlex [1] and the Semantic Scholar Open Data Platform [2] supplies the metadata, abstracts and citation links on which such tools depend; UNKNOWN reads from these sources through a unified chunk schema (Section V-K). C. Claim verification and conflicting evidence In the attribution literature, there have been studies that determine whether the synthesized text is justified by the sources [18]. Verification has been formally defined by FEVER as being based on the extracted evidence [19]. In VeriCite, natural language inference is employed for better citation and CIBER retrieves evidence for and against a claim [20], [21]. Survey on hallucinations provides reasons for this type of task [22]. One area where little work has been done so far is the numerical verification. D. IV. Problem Formulation and Objectives A. Problem statement Let D = {d1, ..., dN} be a collection of academic papers which can include the user’s personal documents and other freely available documents. For a query q, the system should give back the answer a, the collection of sub-queries verdicts and the collection of differences/conflicts and gaps in the form of a report such that all the assertions made in the output are justified by the relevant document or else removed. The query q is broken down into sub-queries q1, ..., qm. The evidence Ei is returned by the retriever for each subquery qi and the sufficiency test gives any of the following three statuses – sufficient, weak and insufficient. B. Research questions RQ1. Is answer accuracy higher and are there less unsupported claims in sufficiency-controlled retrieval compared to single-pass retrieval using the same base retriever? RQ2. How accurate is the claim-level verification in identifying unsupported claims, and how many are fixed or dropped? RQ3. If there are conflicting papers, is reliability weighting presented for both sides together with the rationale? RQ4. How many out-of-date or wrong seeded statements in a user document does the document versus literature comparison reveal? RQ5. Are the limitations stated, implicit gaps and future directions identified properly and are the gap statuses correct? RQ6. What accuracy do source-linked concepts and relations achieve, and what is the latency and cost of the entire pipeline relative to the base retriever and a general assistant with the same documents? RQ7. Is the deterministic confidence score reproducible, and how closely does it match observed correctness, measured by expected calibration error? V. Proposed Methodology A.
