Hybrid retrieval base Both the sub-query on BM25 [7] using the chunk index and on dense retrieval using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model [28] in the FAISS [8] index are applied to each sub-question. The resulting ranked lists are fused using reciprocal rank fusion [9] where chunk c gets a score of score(c) = Σ over lists L of 1 / (k + rank_L(c)) with k as a smoothing parameter. This basic setup is standard and does not vary between any experiments. D. Sufficiency-controlled retrieval For sub-question qi, let Ei denote the top fused chunks and ni be the number of independent source papers among them (two chunks from the same paper are considered one, and papers that cite each other with the same results are marked). ri is the average relevance of Ei as measured by cross-referencing the chunk against qi. The status of the query is defined as status(qi) = sufficient if ni ≥ τn and ri ≥ τr; weak if ni ≥ 1 and ri ≥ τr/2; insufficient otherwise The values of τn and τr are tuned on a development set and reported. In case of insufficient status, the system refactors the query, expands the source base, and repeats the process a certain number of times. If after that the status is insufficient, the sub-question is considered a gap and cannot be answered by the generator from its memory. Every iteration (query variant, sources searched and resulting status) is written to the per-query trace, so that the loop can be audited and ablated. E. Reliability weighting and conflict reporting Each source gets weighted based on the following criteria, w(s) = 0 for retracted; else a·venue(s) + b·recency(s) + g·cites(s) Where venue and recency have the biggest weights, and the citation weight g remains low to minimize the effect of citation count which may affect the result. The retraction criteria are read from metadata if any. In case of contradiction between two evidence sets on the same issue, all sides along with their weights and the probable cause are displayed. Preprints are labelled as such, and a retraction or correction notice in Crossref metadata sets the weight to zero and raises a visible warning. G. Document-versus-world comparison This solution consists of two parts: one where the input consists only of pieces of the user’s document and another where input consists of the Web and the literature. This system matches the statements of a certain topic and classifies each pair into “agree,” “disagree,” and “not addressed.” In the case of “disagree,” both the statements along with the weights indicating their reliability are presented to the user. Web statements are fetched at answer time and stored with their retrieval time and a short verbatim quote span, so that the wording shown to the user can be checked against the original page. H. Three-type research-gap report Extracted gap candidates are stored in three lists: author-claimed limitations, gaps derived from multiple papers, and research directions. The criteria for inclusion of any derived gap include the evidence for such gap and the rationale behind its being a gap, as an author claimed limitation is not necessarily a gap. The document, page, and chunk numbers are listed along with each of the gaps together with their sufficiency level (sufficient, insufficient evidence). I. Open knowledge connectors and unified chunk schema Besides the user’s documents, UNKNOWN is designed to query free and legal sources through their public interfaces: OpenAlex [1], Semantic Scholar [2], arXiv, Crossref, Europe PMC and PubMed, CORE, Unpaywall, DOAJ, Wikipedia and Wikidata. Connectors cache responses, respect rate limits and retry on failure. Only open-access full text or abstracts are used; for other papers just metadata and a link are stored, and nothing behind a paywall is scraped. Every result is converted to one chunk schema holding the text, source type, title, authors, year, venue, DOI, URL, licence, retrieval time, citation count, retraction status, section, character offsets, content hash, and workspace and document identifiers. Records are deduplicated by DOI, title similarity and content hash, so that a paper found in two catalogues counts as one independent source in the sufficiency test. Deterministic confidence score Confidence is computed only in the backend and is returned with every result as a score, a breakdown and a formula version, so the interface never calculates its own value. Four inputs are used, defined in Table V. The score is C = 100 · g( w1·S + w2·E + w3·R + w4·A ) where the weights w1 to w4 are fixed, non-negative and sum to one, and g is a monotone calibration map (isotonic or Platt scaling [29]) fitted on a development set and versioned together with the weights. No sampling is involved, so identical inputs always give an identical score. Calibration quality is reported as expected calibration error [29]. Workspace isolation, deletion and history Each user owns one or more workspaces, and every workspace has its own BM25 index, FAISS index, files, metadata and history, keyed by user and workspace identifiers. A query declares its scope (this document, selected documents, all of the user’s documents, or documents plus web), and retrieval is restricted to that namespace, so a query on one document cannot return chunks from another. History entries store the time, scope, query, feature and a snapshot of the result for each user and document. Results and Discussion A. Verified software results TABLE X. SOFTWARE VERIFICATION These results indicate that the examined software path sequences are functional. They are not retrieval tests and do not give evidence of the relevancy of retrieved passages,answer accuracy, nor do they prove the superior performance of UNKNOWN to other systems. B. Planned measurements TABLE XI. PLANNED MEASUREMENTS (NOT YET RUN) No improvement is claimed until these values come from real runs. C. Illustrative walk-through (design example, not a measured result) To show how the stages interact, consider the query “What are the limitations of BERT-style models for long documents?”. The query is decomposed into three sub-questions: the input-length limit, the computational cost, and the proposed remedies. Suppose several independent open-access papers address the length limit and the remedies, so those two sub-questions are marked sufficient, whereas only one source addresses cost, so that sub-question is marked weak. The loop then reformulates the cost query and widens the set of sources; if the status is still weak after the allowed rounds, cost is reported under “What I could not find” instead of being answered from model memory. During verification, a claim that states a token limit is kept only if that number appears in its cited passage, and an unsupported claim is repaired or dropped. The final report lists the claim labels, any conflict between sources, the confidence score with its breakdown, and the remaining gap. D. Discussion Cost is introduced by the architecture. The additional latency and the number of calls to the language model, resulting from multiple steps of retrieval, verification, and comparison, make it necessary to evaluate if the gain in precision compensates for it. The sufficiency levels are likely to be influenced by the dataset used. The next step will be the ablation analysis presented in Section VII. Live calls to external interfaces add network latency and make results depend on availability, and evidence that comes from abstracts alone is shallower than full text, so such evidence is labelled as

IX. Limitations and Threats to Validity Evidence. The novelty assertion rests on searches that were not exhaustive, and the surveyed papers were assessed from abstracts and the text available to us; they should be read in full, and the search repeated immediately before submission, because this field changes quickly. Verification. Entailment and number verification may be erroneous when dealing with paraphrasing or implicit claims, and the selected passage may be erroneous. Reliability weights. Venue and recency are imperfect surrogates for quality, and retraction information could be incomplete. The weights require tweaking and testing for any bias. Comparison and gaps. Matching a statement in a document against the literature could incorrectly assess scope, while an inferred gap should be confirmed by an expert. A confidence value produced by the model cannot be interpreted as a calibrated probability. The deterministic confidence score is reproducible, but it is not a probability until it has been calibrated on held-out data and its expected calibration error has been reported. Extraction. An asserted node does not automatically mean that it is a correct extraction. Rule-based querying could misclassify a question of ambiguous intent. Data coverage. Only open-access full text and abstracts are used and paywalled papers are never scraped, so some answers rest on abstracts alone. Coverage is far smaller than that of commercial indexes, and results depend on the availability, rate limits and licences of external interfaces. Model dependence. Generation and claim verification depend on the chosen language model and entailment model, whose behaviour can change between versions; each run should therefore record the model versions used. Isolation. Namespace isolation protects stored data inside the application. It does not replace operating-system or network security, and any external language-model provider still receives the retrieved text sent to it. X. Conclusion and Future Work UNKNOWN is a scholarly information retrieval system that uses an evidence-sufficiency signal to control both retrieval and generation, verifies each claim against its cited passage, weights sources by reliability, reports conflicts and differences between a user’s document and the literature, and types and links research gaps to their evidence. It keeps each user’s documents in isolated, deletable workspaces and reports one deterministic confidence score with its breakdown. The retrieval corpus and the hybrid retriever are conventional; the contribution is the control and verification logic around them and its integration into one workflow. Executive Summary This fictional study examines whether a four-week study-planning intervention improves assignment completion among first-year university students. The intervention combines a weekly planning session, short daily check-ins, and a task-prioritization worksheet. In a small pilot, the intervention group completed a larger share of assignments by their deadlines than a comparison group. Because students were not randomly assigned and the sample was small, the results show an association rather than proof that the intervention caused the improvement. 2. Research Question and Hypotheses Primary research question: Is participation in a structured study-planning intervention associated with higher on-time assignment completion over four weeks? H1: Students offered the intervention will have a higher mean on-time assignment completion rate than students receiving usual study guidance. H2: Students who use the planning worksheet on at least three days per week will report greater confidence in managing their workload. H3: The intervention effect may be smaller for students with more than 15 hours of paid work per week. This is exploratory, not a confirmed finding. 3. Methods Design: Four-week, non-randomized pilot study at a fictional university. Participants volunteered after an announcement in two introductory courses. The intervention group included 30 students and the comparison group included 28 students. Group membership followed course scheduling, not random assignment. Intervention: A 20-minute planning workshop at the start of week one; a worksheet asking students to list tasks, deadlines, estimated effort, and priority; and optional daily check-ins taking approximately two minutes. Comparison students received the university’s standard study-skills handout. Measures: The primary outcome was the percentage of recorded assignments submitted by the deadline during the four-week period. The secondary outcome was self-reported workload-management confidence, measured on a 1–5 scale at baseline and week four. Worksheet use was self-reported. Long-term grades, learning retention, and mental health were not measured. Analysis plan: Report group means and percentage-point differences. Because assignment was not randomized and the sample was small, the pilot was treated as descriptive. No causal conclusion was pre-registered. Missing assignment records were excluded from the completion-rate denominator. 4. Results Table 1. Limitations Small sample: only 58 students participated, limiting precision and generalizability. Non-random assignment: pre-existing differences between courses or students may explain some of the observed difference. Self-selection: volunteers may be more motivated than students who did not participate. Short duration: four weeks is not enough to determine whether any improvement persists. Self-reported use: worksheet adherence may be over- or under-reported. Missing data: excluding assignments with missing records may bias the completion-rate estimate if missingness differed between groups. No inferential statistics: the packet provides no p-values, confidence intervals, or adjusted models. 7.
